title: The Orthogonal Score: Why Debiased ML's Bias Multiplies Instead of Adds
summary: Suppose you want to estimate a treatment effect theta0 in the partially linear model
body:
Suppose you want to estimate a treatment effect $\theta_0$ in the partially linear model

$$Y = \theta_0 D + g_0(X) + \varepsilon, \qquad D = m_0(X) + V, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid X, D] = 0,$$

where $D$ is a scalar treatment, $X$ is high-dimensional, and $g_0$ and $m_0$ are unknown. If $X$ were low-dimensional you would run OLS and go home. If it is not, the honest thing is to let a flexible learner — a lasso, a random forest, a boosted tree — estimate $g_0$ and $m_0$, then plug those estimates in. The surprise, which took the field until roughly 2016 to state cleanly, is that *how* you plug them in decides whether you get a root-$n$ consistent estimator or an estimator whose bias is worse than the noise it tries to clean up. Double/debiased machine learning (DML) is a small set of recipes — Neyman-orthogonal scores and cross-fitting — that make the plug-in work. The reason it works is a single algebraic fact: at the truth, the bias from each nuisance error enters the score multiplicatively, not additively.

## Why this matters now

A decade after Robinson's partially linear estimator and two decades after the targeted-learning literature, DML has become the operational default across applied causal inference, policy learning, and the growing seam of computational social science and NLP that treats text as a treatment, an outcome, or a confounder (Feder et al., 2022). It is the engine behind the DoubleML (Bach et al., 2022) and EconML packages, and it is the first thing a modern applied economist reaches for when they need an average effect that an ML residualization can clean. The method is widely used; the orthogonality property that makes it defensible is still often treated as folklore. Spending ten minutes on the derivation is useful, because the folklore misleads in both directions: it sometimes says less than DML delivers (Neyman orthogonality really does give you root-$n$ inference with slow learners), and it sometimes says more (slow learners that converge too slowly, or in a direction correlated with the target residual, break the guarantee).

## The orthogonal score, built from residuals

A moment condition for $\theta_0$ is a function $\psi(W; \theta, \eta)$ of the data $W = (Y, D, X)$, a parameter $\theta$, and a nuisance $\eta$ (collecting $g_0, m_0$), such that at truth

$$\mathbb{E}[\psi(W; \theta_0, \eta_0)] = 0.$$

The $Z$-estimator $\hat{\theta}$ solves the sample version. The naive score for the partially linear model is the OLS score, $\psi_{\mathrm{OLS}}(W; \theta, g) = (Y - \theta D - g(X)) D$. It identifies $\theta_0$ but has a fatal property: a perturbation $g = g_0 + r \Delta_g$ changes $\mathbb{E}[\psi]$ to first order in $r$, so the plug-in's bias is first-order in the ML error $\hat{g} - g_0$. ML errors shrink at rates like $n^{-1/4}$ or $n^{-1/3}$, not $n^{-1/2}$, so first-order sensitivity leaves a bias that dominates the variance.

Neyman's fix is to pick a moment that is *first-order insensitive* to the nuisance at the truth. Formally, the Gateaux derivative along any direction $\Delta$ vanishes:

$$\partial_r \, \mathbb{E}\!\left[\psi(W; \theta_0, \eta_0 + r \Delta)\right]\Big|_{r=0} = 0.$$

For the partially linear model this is realized by Robinson's residual-on-residual score (Robinson, 1988; Chernozhukov et al., 2018),

$$\psi(W; \theta, g, m) = \big(Y - g(X) - \theta\, (D - m(X))\big)\big(D - m(X)\big).$$

Two quick observations. First, at $\theta = \theta_0$ and $(g,m) = (g_0, m_0)$ the two factors are $\varepsilon$ and $V$, which are uncorrelated given $X$, so $\mathbb{E}[\psi] = 0$: the score identifies $\theta_0$. Second, perturbing $g$ by $\Delta_g$ at the truth gives $\mathbb{E}[-\Delta_g(X)\,V] = 0$ because $V$ is mean-zero conditional on $X$; perturbing $m$ by $\Delta_m$ gives $\mathbb{E}[-\theta_0 \Delta_m \cdot V - \varepsilon \Delta_m] = 0$ by the same argument. Both Gateaux derivatives vanish. The score is Neyman-orthogonal to $(g, m)$.

The algebra of what this buys you is cleanest in the bias expansion. Writing $\hat\eta - \eta_0 = (\hat g - g_0, \hat m - m_0)$ and expanding around the truth,

$$\mathbb{E}[\psi(W; \theta_0, \hat\eta)] = \mathbb{E}[\psi(W; \theta_0, \eta_0)] + \underbrace{\partial_\eta \mathbb{E}[\psi]\cdot(\hat\eta - \eta_0)}_{= 0 \text{ by orthogonality}} + \tfrac{1}{2} \partial^2_\eta \mathbb{E}[\psi] \cdot (\hat\eta - \eta_0)^2 + \ldots$$

The second-order term, for Robinson's score, is $\mathbb{E}[(\hat g - g_0)(\hat m - m_0)]$ — the inner product of the two nuisance errors. The bias is a *product* of the two errors, not a sum. If each converges at rate $n^{-1/4}$, the product converges at $n^{-1/2}$, matching the variance scale. The naive score, by contrast, has bias $\mathbb{E}[(\hat g - g_0) D]$, which is first-order in a single nuisance and does not vanish fast enough. This is the entire reason DML can afford to use ML.

## Cross-fitting: the second ingredient

Orthogonality alone is not enough. If you fit $\hat g$ and $\hat m$ on the same observations where you later evaluate the score, you reintroduce overfitting bias that no amount of orthogonality fixes. Cross-fitting is the trivial-looking remedy. Partition the data into $K$ folds. For each fold $k$, estimate $\hat g^{(-k)}, \hat m^{(-k)}$ on the complement, then evaluate $\psi$ on fold $k$ using those out-of-fold nuisances. The point is independence: the fitted nuisance on an observation is a function of other observations only, so its error does not conspire with the score's residuals. Average $\psi$ over all folds and solve for $\theta$ (DML2 in Chernozhukov et al. (2018); DML1 solves per-fold and averages the estimators). Chernozhukov et al. recommend DML2 for its empirical stability.

With both ingredients, the main result is clean (Chernozhukov et al., 2018, Theorem 3.1): under regularity, if $\|\hat g - g_0\|_2 \cdot \|\hat m - m_0\|_2 = o_P(n^{-1/2})$ — satisfied whenever each nuisance converges at $o_P(n^{-1/4})$ in $L_2$ — the DML estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-asymptotically normal with the semiparametric efficiency bound as its variance, and valid confidence intervals come from the sample variance of the score at the plug-in.

## A concrete anchor

Here is a 15-line NumPy sketch — enough to see the effect move with your own eyes.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n, p = 2000, 50
X = rng.standard_normal((n, p))
beta_m = rng.standard_normal(p) * (np.arange(p) < 5)   # sparse propensity
beta_g = rng.standard_normal(p) * (np.arange(p) < 5)   # sparse outcome
m0 = X @ beta_m
D = m0 + rng.standard_normal(n)
g0 = X @ beta_g
Y = 1.5 * D + g0 + rng.standard_normal(n)              # true theta_0 = 1.5
m_hat = LassoCV(cv=5).fit(X, D).predict(X)             # same-sample, no CF
g_hat = LassoCV(cv=5).fit(X, Y).predict(X)
V = D - m_hat; U = Y - g_hat
print("naive OLS plug-in :", (D * (Y - g_hat)).sum() / (D * D).sum())
print("orthogonal, no CF :", (U * V).sum() / (V * V).sum())
# Replace the two Lasso fits with 5-fold out-of-sample predictions; the
# orthogonal estimator shrinks to 1.5 within sampling noise. The naive one
# does not.
```

The orthogonal score with cross-fitting lands near the truth; the naive plug-in sits a visible distance above it, and the gap does not shrink when you grow $n$ at a fixed sparsity. The failure mode is that in-sample Lasso residuals are not pure noise — they are shrunk by the penalty — and the naive score pays for the first-order dependence.

## What it implies in practice

Three operational choices follow. First, when you reach for a flexible nuisance learner inside a causal estimator, write the moment in orthogonal form before fitting anything: residualize both $Y$ and $D$ on $X$, regress residuals on residuals. The DoubleML and EconML packages do this by default, but hand-rolled pipelines often do not, and the price is first-order bias from any regularization. Second, always cross-fit — five folds is the usual choice and the two-fold "DML1" is an acceptable fallback at small $n$. The computational cost is $K$ times the single fit; the inference cost of skipping it is losing your confidence intervals. Third, remember that DML gives you the *average* effect under the specified model. For heterogeneity you need a different orthogonal moment — for example the double-ML flavour of the R-learner, or causal-forest-style local orthogonalization.

## Limits and open questions

The product-of-errors story is a sufficient condition, not necessary, and it has three real limits. First, the $n^{-1/4}$ rate is a $L_2$ assumption; a nuisance that converges in a weaker norm or whose error is correlated with $V$ at the fine scale can still break the inference even when the headline rate looks fine. Second, higher-order orthogonality — making the bias third-order — is not free: Mackey, Syrgkanis, and Zadik (2018) showed that in the partially linear setting a second-order orthogonal moment exists only when the treatment residual $V$ is non-Gaussian, by a Stein-identity argument, so for Gaussian treatment one really is stuck at the product rate. Third, DML buys root-$n$ inference for a scalar functional of the distribution; for CATEs the achievable rate reverts to the slower nonparametric rate and the orthogonality story has to be redone around a target function rather than a scalar. On the applied side, DML inherits every identification assumption of the underlying model — unconfoundedness, SUTVA, correct specification of what the nuisance is conditioning on — and treats them as given. The method debiases ML estimation; it does not debias your causal design. A related and under-appreciated failure mode is weak overlap: when the propensity $m_0(X)$ gets near the boundary of its support, the inverse-variance weights implicit in the orthogonal score blow up and the asymptotic normality relies on tail conditions that modern tabular benchmarks rarely satisfy; trimming helps the variance but reintroduces a bias the orthogonal score was supposed to kill. The honest reading is that DML is a sharp instrument on a well-posed design, and a bad instrument everywhere else.

## Further reading

- Chernozhukov, V., Chetverikov, D., Demirer, M., Duflo, E., Hansen, C., Newey, W., Robins, J. (2018). *Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Structural Parameters.* The Econometrics Journal, 21(1), C1–C68. <https://doi.org/10.1111/ectj.12097>. The reference statement of DML, Neyman orthogonality, and cross-fitting; the result above is Theorem 3.1.
- Robinson, P. M. (1988). *Root-N-Consistent Semiparametric Regression.* Econometrica, 56(4), 931–954. <https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912705>. The residual-on-residual estimator for the partially linear model that the DML score inherits.
- Ahrens, A., Chernozhukov, V., Hansen, C., Kozbur, D., Schaffer, M., Wiemann, T. (2025). *An Introduction to Double/Debiased Machine Learning.* arXiv:2504.08324. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08324>. A current pedagogical treatment with worked examples; forthcoming in the Journal of Economic Literature.
- Mackey, L., Syrgkanis, V., Zadik, I. (2018). *Orthogonal Machine Learning: Power and Limitations.* ICML 2018; arXiv:1711.00342. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00342>. The counterpart to the main result: when higher-order orthogonality is and is not available, and why Gaussian treatment residuals are the obstruction.
- Bach, P., Chernozhukov, V., Kurz, M. S., Spindler, M. (2022). *DoubleML — An Object-Oriented Implementation of Double Machine Learning in Python.* arXiv:2104.03220. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.03220>. The software companion; useful to read as a worked specification of the score and the cross-fitting loop.
- Feder, A. et al. (2022). *Causal Inference in Natural Language Processing: Estimation, Prediction, Interpretation and Beyond.* Transactions of the ACL, 10. <https://aclanthology.org/2022.tacl-1.66/>. The survey that places DML inside the NLP causal-inference landscape, including text-as-treatment settings where its orthogonality guarantees do and do not transfer.
